panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial post-contrast CT in 65-year-old female described as well-defined circumscribed intraconal lesion between medial rectus and optic nerve with proptosis and early focal stippled enhancement, stated as characteristic of CVM/venous malformation. B: Coronal post-contrast CT of same 65-year-old female lesion as panel A, described as characteristic of CVM/venous malformation. Same proposed lesion finding as no CT vocabulary entry exists. panels.figure_caption: Axial (a) and coronal (b) post-contrast CT image of the orbits in a 65-year-old female patient demonstrates a well-defined, circumscribed, intraconal lesion in the left orbit located between the medial rectus muscle and the optic nerve, with associated proptosis and mild globe indentation. The lesion exhibits early focal stippled enhancement following contrast administration. These imaging features are characteristic of a CVM. (c) Axial non-contrast CT of a 16-year-old female patient with left orbital venous malformation, showing multiple well-circumscribed hyperdense round foci within the intraconal lesion, consistent with phleboliths, a typical finding in venous malformations.
in_text_mentions: ated within the intraconal space, usually lateral to the optic nerve. They are isoattenuating or slightly hyperattenuating relative to extraocular muscles. A hallmark feature of CVM is delayed progressive enhancement: initial focal peripheral or central enhancement which gradually progresses to incomplete or heterogeneous filling in delayed phases. This “centripetal” enhancement pattern reflects their slow-flow vascular channels and helps differentiate CVMs from other orbital tumors (see Figure 1) such as schwannomas or lymphomas. In 88.5% of cases, delayed incomplete filling is noted (9, 12).

panels.figure_caption: In surgery, the soft cystic mass was dissected from the overlying skin. It did not extend to the conchal cartilage and was completely removed. On histopathology, irregularly dilated venous channels with sparse smooth muscle cells without arteries were observed (hematoxylin-eosin, ×100). Thus, venous malformation was diagnosed. Six months after surgery, the wound had healed well and there was no recurrence.

in_text_mentions: A 25-year-old woman first presented a painful, progressively enlarging mass on the sole of her left foot 20 years ago, which was associated with overlying erythema. Non-contrast MRI revealed a 4 × 3 cm lobulated subcutaneous lesion along the lateral plantar aspect that was isointense on T1-weighted imaging (T1-WI) and hyperintense on fat-suppressed T2-WI (Figure 1). Based on the MRI findings, hemangioma and arteriovenous malformation were ruled out, and the final diagnosis was left lower-limb PVM.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E of intrathyroidal cavernous hemangioma showing thin-walled dilated vascular spaces, attributed to venous_malformation per article topic and caption. B: Low-power H&E showing congested varying-caliber vascular channels of cavernous hemangioma, consistent with dilated venous channels histology. C: Medium-power H&E showing cavernous vascular spaces with entrapped thyroid follicles, diagnostic of intrathyroidal cavernous hemangioma. D: High-power H&E highlighting flat bland endothelium lining lesional vessels with red cells, supporting dilated venous channels histology.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic features of intrathyroidal cavernous hemangioma (Case 2). (A) Low-power photomicrograph depicting an unencapsulated but circumscribed, lobular proliferation of numerous, thin-walled, vascular spaces. (B) Low-power photomicrograph showing numerous, congested, varying-in-caliber vascular channels. (C) Medium-power photomicrograph showing entrapped residual thyroid follicles among the cavernous vascular spaces. (D) High-power photomicrograph highlighting the monolayer of flattened, cytologically bland, endothelial cells lining the lesional vessels
in_text_mentions: g ~ 50% of the cut surface of the specimen was noted upon sectioning. Microscopically, the lesion comprised an unencapsulated but circumscribed, lobular proliferation of numerous, thin-walled, vascular spaces (Fig. 3A and B), in the vicinity of a follicular adenoma. The congested, varying-in-caliber, vascular channels (Fig. 3B and C) were lined by a monolayer of flattened, bland, endothelial cells (Fig. 3D). Entrapped residual follicles were noted among the cavernous vascular spaces (Fig. 3C). A diagnosis of cavernous hemangioma of the thyroid in association with a follicular adenoma was made.

panels.rationale: Single axial T2 MRI shows well-defined hyperintense left orbital lesion with arrow, captioned as cavernous hemangioma in article titled Conservative Management of a Slow-Flow Orbital Cavernous Hemangioma with primary disease venous_malformation, matching T2 lobulated lesion vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Habbash. Conservative Management of a Slow-Flow Orbital Cavernous Hemangioma: A Case Report.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.72309. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Axial MRI T2-weighted image demonstrating a well-defined, hyperintense intraconal lesion in the left orbit, consistent with a cavernous hemangioma (arrow) The lesion is causing mild proptosis without evidence of optic nerve compression or infiltration of adjacent structures.
in_text_mentions: y, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbits with contrast was performed, which demonstrated a well-circumscribed, lobulated mass measuring approximately 2.5 cm in the superomedial quadrant of the left orbit. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted images and showed heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration. The mass was located extraconally, displacing the optic nerve inferiorly but without direct involvement or compression. These imaging characteristics were highly suggestive of a cavernous hemangioma, a benign vascular lesion commonly seen in the orbit (Figures 1-4).

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological examination of the excised lesion stained with Masson's trichrome (original magnification ×40). The lesion consisted of multiple large, blood-filled dilated vascular channels separated by fibrous connective tissue septa and lined by a single layer of flattened endothelial cells without cytological atypia or mitotic activity. No evidence of thrombosis, necrosis, or malignancy was observed. These histopathological findings are compatible with a cavernous-type venous vascular lesion (historically referred to as cavernous hemangioma). Immunohistochemical staining was not performed
in_text_mentions: Hemostasis was achieved after releasing the tourniquet, and the wound was closed without tension. No skin graft or flap reconstruction was necessary. Histopathological examination revealed the presence of hemangioma with no signs of atypia and clear resection margins (Figure 5).

source_variant.figure_caption: Histopathological examination of the excised lesion stained with Masson's trichrome (original magnification ×40). The lesion consisted of multiple large, blood-filled dilated vascular channels separated by fibrous connective tissue septa and lined by a single layer of flattened endothelial cells without cytological atypia or mitotic activity. No evidence of thrombosis, necrosis, or malignancy was observed. These histopathological findings are compatible with a cavernous-type venous vascular lesion (historically referred to as cavernous hemangioma). Immunohistochemical staining was not performed

in_text_mentions: not palpable in the rest of the neck. Routine laboratory blood investigations were done which were within normal limits. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E of resected anal canal lesion shows dilated blood-filled vascular spaces lined by flattened endothelium, matching venous malformation histology vocabulary. B: CD34 IHC of same resected cavernous hemangioma highlights endothelial lining of dilated vascular spaces, supporting venous malformation attribution.
panels.attribution_text: Merchan et al. Cavernous Hemangioma of the Anal Canal Mimicking a Neoplasm: A Rare Cause of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding Successfully Treated With Transanal Excision.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.84214. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological examination of the resected lesion (A) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (10×) reveals large, dilated, blood-filled vascular spaces lined by a single layer of flattened endothelial cells, consistent with cavernous hemangioma. (B) Immunohistochemistry for CD34 (10×) shows strong membranous positivity in the endothelial lining of the vascular spaces, confirming their vascular nature.
in_text_mentions: The postoperative course was uneventful. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 1. Final pathology confirmed complete resection of a cavernous hemangioma, with immunohistochemical staining positive for CD34 in vascular endothelium and a Ki-67 index of 2%, supporting a benign vascular lesion (Figure 3). Follow-up visits at three and 12 weeks included rigid rectosigmoidoscopy, which showed normal mucosal healing with no evidence of recurrence or residual lesion.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Panel a is axial T2 fat-sat MRI showing cluster-like intraarticular intrasynovial venous malformation in 7-year-old boy, as captioned. Real patient MRI with textbook T2 hyperintense lesion. b: Panel b sagittal T2 shows same cluster-like venous malformation invading fat pads and synovial cavity, supporting T2 lobulated lesion finding. c: Panel c post-contrast MRI shows same venous malformation with mild partial enhancement, typical progressive enhancement pattern described in caption. Visual lesion corresponds to vocabulary MRI lesion; enhancement detailed as proposed finding. d: Panel d coronal post-contrast MRI shows more extensive enhancement of same venous malformation with filling defects due to intraluminal thrombosis often present in venous malformations.

panels.figure_caption: A 7-year-old boy with an intraarticular and intrasynovial venous malformation of the knee. a, b Axial (a) and sagittal (b) T2-weighted fat-saturated MR images. The cluster-like venous malformation protrudes into the suprapatellar recess (arrow in a). A mild synovial effusion with post-hemorrhage debris is present (arrowhead in a). The venous malformation invades both the suprapatellar and infrapatellar fat pads (arrows in b) as well as the intrasynovial cavity (arrowhead in b). c, d T1-weighted fat-saturated post-contrast axial (c) and coronal (d) MR images demonstrate the progressive enhancement typical for venous malformations. The first post-contrast image (c) shows only mild and partial enhancement of the venous malformation (arrow). A consecutively obtained coronal image (d) demonstrates more extensive enhancement. The filling defects (arrow in d) are due to intraluminal thrombosis often present in venous malformations

The lesion morphology was well demarcated and cluster-like in half of the patients (Figs. 2 and 3), the other half being diffuse and phlebectatic (Figs. 4 and 5). The enhancement pattern after gadolinium was partial and progressively increased in consecutive sequences in 10 patients (Fig. 3). However, in diffuse lesions with narrower vascular spaces, the enhancement was intense beginning from the first post-contrast images (Fig. 5). Phleboliths or thrombosis was present in 79% of the lesions

/14 patients) (86%) (Fig. 2). Overall, the venous malformation appeared intracapsular but extrasynovial in 7 patients (50%) and intracapsular with intrasynovial extension in the remaining 7 (Figs. 2, 3, 4 and 5). A synovial effusion was present in 4 patients (29%), all with intrasynovial involvement (Fig. 3). Three of the 7 clearly intrasynovial lesions (43%) were associated with established chondral damage, characterized by thinning of the articular surface cartilage, full thickness cartilage defects and osteochondral lesions (Fig. 4). Permanent histopathologic examination of the tumor showed large blood-filled spaces lined with flattened endothelium, and the tumor was found to be a VM, so-called cavernous hemangioma (Figure 3). The postoperative course was uneventful. The endoscopic view revealed preservation of both the inferior turbinates (Figure 4). Postoperative CT showed that both sides of the nasolacrimal ducts and inferior turbinates were preserved (Figure 5). Nasal breathing was found to be satisfactory. No nasolacrimal duct obstruction was observed. The patient showed no evidence of disease recurrence

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial T1WI shows hypointense cavernous sinus mass in patient with article-title diagnosis of cavernous sinus venous malformation; caption explicitly attributes panel A to this lesion. B: Axial T2WI shows hyperintense cavernous sinus mass matching venous malformation T2 hyperintense lesion vocabulary; caption and in-text support hyperintensity on T2WI uniformly distributed. C: Coronal T2 FLAIR shows marked hyperintense cavernous sinus mass; FLAIR is T2-weighted and supports T2 hyperintense lesion finding for venous malformation. D: Post-contrast axial MRI shows marked and even enhancement of the cavernous sinus mass in confirmed cavernous sinus venous malformation case; enhancement pattern not in vocabulary so captured as proposed finding.

in_text_mentions: dings from the imaging examinations, the final imaging diagnosis suggests the possibility of a meningioma. The patient underwent cavernous sinus brain tumour resection under general anaesthesia. Intraoperatively, the tumour was identified in the cavernous sinus area, appearing as a semi-transparent grey-red mass with a diameter of approximately 2 cm. The postoperative pathological report revealed that the lumen was composed of numerous blood vessels, varying in size, with uneven thickness of the vessel walls (Figure 4). The final pathological diagnosis is a cavernous sinus venous malformation.

panels.rationale: Single B-mode ultrasound shows hypoechoic polilobulated compressible lesion of left cheek explicitly diagnosed as thrombosed venous malformation in caption and in-text, matching compressible channels on ultrasound vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Álvaro-Martinez et al. Venous malformation differential diagnosis with an odontogenic abscess on a pediatric patient. Case report and review of the literature.. Journal of clinical and experimental dentistry 2024. doi:10.4317/jced.61416. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Ultrasound images. Lesion on B mode. Echography of the left cheek: polilobulated hypoechogenic lesion, well defined and embedded in deep layer of subcutaneous tissue anterior to masticatory muscles without infiltration of approximately 1x2x3 cm. It is compressible. On its lateral left side, there are two small vessels with phasic flow suggestive of veins and it does not present flow on Doppler Mode. Taking into account the clinical and radiologic correlate, the lesion is suggestive of a thrombosed venous malformation.
in_text_mentions: rted. Based on these findings, the main diagnosis was a soft tissue tumor, of probable vascular origin due to the skin discoloration. Given this suspicion, an echography was requested, which confirmed a thrombosed venous malformation, measuring 1x2,3x3cm, located superficial to the masticatory muscles (Figs. 2,3). The patient was prescribed aspirin, 125 mg/24 hours for three months to resolve the thrombotic event, and was included in the Committee for Congenital Vascular Malformations to decide on an interdisciplinary management. A conservative approach was agreed upon with clinical follow up.

source_variant.figure_caption: Ultrasound images. Lesion before and after compression; Lesion on doppler Mode. Echography of the left cheek: polilobulated hypoechogenic lesion, well defined and embedded in deep layer of subcutaneous tissue anterior to masticatory muscles without infiltration of approximately 1x2x3 cm. It is compressible. On its lateral left side, there are two small vessels with phasic flow suggestive of veins and it does not present flow on Doppler Mode. Taking into account the clinical and radiologic correlate, the lesion is suggestive of a thrombosed venous malformation.

panels.attribution_text: Kim et al. Management Considerations in Nasal Bone Intraosseous Cavernous Hemangioma: A Case Report and Literature Review.. Case reports in medicine 2026. doi:10.1155/carm/1774878. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histologic findings revealed several dilated blood vessels with a single layer of vascular space between the bony trabeculas (× 100).
in_text_mentions: Despite being benign, the patient wanted surgical excision due to the epiphora and cosmetic concerns. The mass was removed completely from the area between the nasal bone, orbit, and nasolacrimal duct using an external incision that did not injure the nasal mucosa. A well‐encapsulated mass was removed with minimal bleeding, and the site was healed without a flap or bone graft. Histological analysis revealed an expanded, dilated vascular space between bony trabeculas and fibrous stroma, with no indications of malignancy (Figure 3).

plate_findings.evidence: Ultrasound image showing hypoechoic thickening of the right frontal calvarium with irregular cortical surface (yellow arrowheads)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Grayscale ultrasound of histologically confirmed calvarial venous malformation showing hypoechoic thickening/compressible cavities, matching compressible channels vocabulary. B: Compression ultrasound directly demonstrates compressible venous cavities of venous malformation. C: Decompression ultrasound counterpart showing re-expansion of compressible cavities of same venous malformation. D: CT shows expansile osteolytic lesion of right frontal bone with radiating trabeculae creating sunburst/honeycomb appearance, confirmed as intraosseous venous malformation histologically; no CT vocabulary term exists so captured as proposed finding. E: Color Doppler during compression shows low-flow vascular channels with forward flow, interpreted as low-flow vascular malformation. F: Color Doppler during decompression shows vascular reflux/inversion of flow color, characteristic low-flow venous malformation phenomenon.
panels.attribution_text: Messaoudi et al. Calvarial venous malformation highlighted by the flow-reflux phenomenon on ultrasound.. Journal of the Belgian Society of Radiology 2026. doi:10.5334/jbsr.4220. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Calvarial venous malformation of the right frontal bone. A: Ultrasound image showing hypoechoic thickening of the right frontal calvarium with irregular cortical surface (yellow arrowheads). B, C: Ultrasound during compression (B) and decompression (C) demonstrating compressible cavities (yellow arrowheads). D: CT image showing an expansile osteolytic lesion of the right frontal bone with radiating trabeculae, creating a sunburst/honeycomb appearance. E, F: Color Doppler ultrasound during compression (E) and decompression (F) demonstrating a flow–reflux phenomenon with inversion of flow color during ther maneuver (arrowheads).
in_text_mentions: Ultrasound revealed a small, heterogeneous, hypoechoic nodular mass beneath the galea overlying a focal irregular surface of the underlying frontal bone (Figure 1A). The mass was slightly compressible (Figures 1B and 1D). No vascular signal was observed on color Doppler imaging. However, dynamic assessment with gentle compression with the transducer induced forward flow within the cavities, and vascular reflux during decompression (Figures 1E and 1F). This flow–reflux phenomenon was interpreted as suggestive of a low‑flow vascular malformation.

Computed tomography (CT) confirmed an expansile osteolytic lesion of the right frontal bone, composed of thin radiating trabeculae creating a characteristic sunburst appearance (Figure 1D). These imaging findings were consistent with an intraosseous vascular malformation, which was confirmed histologically after resection.

in_text_mentions: During surgical excision, the mass was found to be encapsulated by MR fibres. The MR fibres were separated and the mass was removed completely. The MR fibres were sutured together with 6-0 vicryl suture. The mass measuring 20 × 8 × 6.5 mm was removed and sent for histopathology. The histopathological examination revealed an intramuscular cavernous hemangioma (Figure 4). The patient was started on oral steroids for two weeks to ameliorate the postoperative edema and fibrosis.

Gross examination of mass showed a rubbery round tissue with measurement of 3.5×2.8×2 cm, and cut sections showed dark red brown surface with microcytic appearance. in_text_mentions: AC mass was excised in bloc by elevating the skin in continuity with the lesion. The healthy surrounding skin 2 mm from the tumor margin was also removed. in_text_mentions: nd was finally diagnosed as venous malformation. In October, 2019, his mother was referred to radiologists for consultation. B-scan imaging at that time showed a low-echo mass in his left cheek (Fig. 1A). However, angiographic examination was not conducted. After that, the boy underwent percutaneous injection of 5 ml 3% polidocanol to the subcutaneous mass in his left cheek. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is T1WI MRI of anterior mediastinal mass in article titled Venous Malformation in the Anterior Mediastinum; caption states mass appeared isointense on T1WI (A) with no flow voids, supporting VM attribution. T1 appearance has no vocabulary key, recorded as proposed finding. B: Panel B is T2WI MRI of same anterior mediastinal mass; caption and in-text state hyperintense on T2WI without flow voids, with imaging suggesting VM, directly supporting T2 hyperintense lesion finding.
panels.attribution_text: Sakai et al. Venous Malformation in the Anterior Mediastinum.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.58581. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) and T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) MRI The mass appeared isointense on T1WI (A) and hyperintense on T2WI (B), with no observed flow voids.
in_text_mentions: as a new finding. Despite having no symptoms, an unenhanced CT showed an anterior mediastinal mass with sparse calcification (Figure 1). On MRI, the mass appeared isointense on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) without flow voids (Figure 2). Dynamic enhanced CT later revealed early and persistent enhancement with contrast material accumulation in the delayed phase, but the arterial inflow of the contrast remained unknown (Figure 3). While the imaging suggested a VM, the possibility of an AVM/F could not be ruled out due to the early enhancement observed.

panels.figure_caption: Endoscopic features of the lesion.
in_text_mentions: After performing colonoscopy for hematochezia, a 49-year-old woman was referred to our center. A subepithelial lesion, approximately 18–20 mm, with a bluish rim and superficial congestion, was found in the rectum ( Fig. 1 ). EUS (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) showed a submucosal, non-homogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic lesion, with anechoic areas and calcification with an acoustic shadow ( Fig. 2 a, b ). Magnetic resonance imaging showed a T2 hyperintense neoplasm ( Fig. 3 a, b ). A submucosal vascular tumor was suspected; thus, ESD was scheduled.

in_text_mentions: ESD with a HybridKnife (Erbe, Tübingen, Germany) ( Video 1 ) was performed. Given the suspicion of a vascular lesion, the procedure was carried out with great caution to avoid major bleeding. Saline-immersion therapeutic and prophylactic vessel coagulation was performed, as recently described 4 . The patient was discharged asymptomatic the day after. Histological examination confirmed a submucosal cavernous hemangioma with free resection margins ( Fig. 4 a, b ).

in_text_mentions: He had been managed conservatively with beta-blockers and steroids elsewhere for years with no appreciable benefit. General examination was normal. in_text_mentions: A 55-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of intermittent dizziness, which could be relieved by rest and was not accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and sight rotation. She was otherwise healthy and had no history of chronic diseases such as hypertension and diabetes. She was initially diagnosed at a neurology clinic and was referred for a whole-brain MR scan, which revealed an intrasellar mass (Fig. 1a and b). The patient was referred to our neurosurgery department for further diagnosis and treatment.

enhanced MR scan of the pituitary revealed an abnormal ellipsoid signal in the sellar region with dimensions of 2.7 cm × 1.7 cm and a clear boundary. The lesion was located mostly in the intrasellar region but had pushed the optic chiasm slightly upward and invaded the left cavernous sinus. It appeared isointense relative to the gray matter on T1-weighted images (Fig. 1a and c) and hyperintense on T2-weighted images (Fig. 1b and d). An injection of gadolinium contrast revealed heterogeneous enhancement with a mulberry-like appearance (Fig. 1e and f), consistent with a well-vascularized lesion.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: EUS panel a of rectal cavernous hemangioma in 49-year-old woman showing submucosal predominantly hypoechoic lesion with anechoic areas, matching compressible slow-flow channels on ultrasound. b: EUS panel b of same rectal cavernous hemangioma showing the submucosal hypoechoic lesion with internal calcification with acoustic shadow, consistent with venous malformation channels; calcification not in ultrasound vocabulary so listed as proposed.

in_text_mentions: After performing colonoscopy for hematochezia, a 49-year-old woman was referred to our center. A subepithelial lesion, approximately 18–20 mm, with a bluish rim and superficial congestion, was found in the rectum ( Fig. 1 ). EUS (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) showed a submucosal, non-homogeneous, predominantly hypoechoic lesion, with anechoic areas and calcification with an acoustic shadow ( Fig. 2 a, b ). Magnetic resonance imaging showed a T2 hyperintense neoplasm ( Fig. 3 a, b ). A submucosal vascular tumor was suspected; thus, ESD was scheduled.

in_text_mentions: Obtaining a differential diagnosis is best achieved through computed tomography (CT), especially with the use of contrast dye that allows for the enhancement of the hemangioma. However, it is common for patients to sustain both magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and CT as our patient did2,5 (Fig 1). Color Doppler and angiography may also help in the identification.5,6 A definitive diagnosis of orbital cavernous venous malformations requires surgical excision with confirmatory pathological analysis. However, the utilization of MRI and CT can help narrow the differential diagnosis.

panels.rationale: Single MRI panel in disease-focused article on cavernous hemangioma (venous malformation) with caption-specific retro-orbital inferior-medial tumor mass visibly corresponding to orbital lesion causing protrusion in 40-year-old female.
panels.attribution_text: Almeida et al. Cavernous Hemangioma in the Orbital Cavity: Case Report.. European journal of dentistry 2022. doi:10.1055/s-0041-1732948. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging showing retro-orbital and inferior-medial tumor mass.
in_text_mentions: A 40-year-old female patient presented to the head and neck surgery service with a report of protrusion of the right eyeball in early 2019. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) exam was requested to complement the diagnosis, showing a tumor mass positioned in a retro-orbital and inferior-medial form ( Fig. 1 ). The case was treated by excision of the tumor through infraorbital access in the direct hemi-face and remained asymptomatic for 6 months.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Grayscale abdominal ultrasound panel of patient with small intestinal cavernous hemangioma/segmental venous malformation per caption and article title; shows stiff thickened jejunal wall described in caption. B: Color Doppler ultrasound same jejunal segmental venous malformation showing abundant periwall flow signals, supporting low-flow vascular channels. C: Enhanced abdominal CT coronal view showing focal jejunal wall thickening with tortuous chaotic vascular shadows with coronary sign, diagnosed as venous malformation of small intestine per caption. D: Enhanced abdominal CT axial view same lesion showing thickened wall and cross-sectional vascular shadows supplied by superior mesenteric artery, indicating small intestinal venous malformation.

plate_findings.evidence: high signal intensity on T2 weighted and fat suppression images with calcification (a,b)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Axial MRI shows lobulated septated high T2 signal mass in biceps muscle, described as specific for cavernous hemangioma recurrence / venous malformation. b: Longitudinal fat-suppressed T2 MRI shows hyperintense lobulated septated lesion with punctate signal voids related to phleboliths, specific for venous malformation. c: Axial T1 MRI shows same lobulated septated biceps muscle mass with intermediate signal, part of same venous malformation figure; morphology visible though sequence is T1.
panels.attribution_text: Ciurea et al. Role of MRI in the diagnosis and evaluation of cavernous hemangioma of the arm.. Journal of medicine and life 2014. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: 1.5T MRI showing lobulated and septated tumor in the biceps brachial muscles, with high signal intensity on T2 weighted and fat suppression images with calcification (a,b); intermediate signal on T1 weighted images (c)
in_text_mentions: The MRI exam demonstrated round-oval heterogeneous signal tumor mass in the biceps brachial muscles, with high signal intensity on T2 weighted images and septa (Fig. 2a). On T1 weighted images, the tumor had an intermediate signal with diffuse areas of fat increased signal (Fig. 2b). On T2 fat-sat sequences, punctuate signal voids areas related to phleboliths can be seen (Fig. 2c). The imaging features were specific for the recurrence of hemangioma, therefore gadolinium was not administered.

panels.body_site: left frontal skull and left orbit
panels.rationale: Single coronal T1 contrast-enhanced MRI from case of intraosseous orbital cavernous hemangioma. Caption and in-text describe 5cm mass in left frontal skull extending into orbital rim/orbit with globe displacement. Image shows large lobulated left-sided mass, attributed to venous_malformation per article title and in-text stating imaging consistent with hemangioma. Tagged with closest MRI vocabulary finding based on visual lobulated lesion.
panels.attribution_text: Akhter et al. Intraosseous Orbital Cavernous Hemangioma with Frontal Extension and Dural Involvement.. Cureus 2019. doi:10.7759/cureus.4823. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative coronal T1 contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging
in_text_mentions: cm x 4.4 cm mass in the left frontal skull extending into the left orbital rim and into the left orbit with a displacement of the superior rectus muscle and downward displacement of the globe (Figure 1). The mass also indented the inferior left frontal lobe. A fine needle aspiration (FNA) of the soft tissue component in the left superior orbit was performed. Cytology report was compatible with a hematoma and was negative for a neoplasm. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the head without contrast demonstrated a well-circumscribed, expansile 5.3 cm x 3.7 cm x 4.5 cm mass with coarse internal tr

lae [12]. MRI of these lesions shows intermediate to high T1 signal intensity and high heterogeneous T2 signal intensity [9]. There is an extensive differential diagnosis for intradiploic skull masses, including metastatic diseases, meningiomas, sarcomas, dermoid tumors, fibrous dysplasia, Paget disease, etc. [14]. MRI and CT findings, therefore, may not be pathognomonic or sufficient to make a definite preoperative diagnosis. As such, confirmatory diagnosis is made via surgery and biopsy [9]. Our patient presented with imaging on CT and MRI that was consistent with a hemangioma (Figures 1-2).

panels.rationale: Single USG B-scan from disease-focused article on intramuscular cavernous hemangioma of medial rectus, caption describes heterogenous extraconal mass corresponding to venous malformation; real patient ultrasound showing mass with measurement calipers.
panels.attribution_text: Mehta et al. Intramuscular Cavernous Hemangioma of Medial Rectus Muscle in Paediatric Age Group.. Case reports in ophthalmological medicine 2017. doi:10.1155/2017/1076404. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: USG B-scan of orbit showing heterogenous mass in the extraconal compartment close to the insertion of the medial rectus.
in_text_mentions: USG B-scan revealed a heterogenous mass approximately 23 × 13 mm in extraconal compartment close to the insertion of the medial rectus (MR) muscle with few hyperechoic flecks (Figure 2). MRI of the orbit revealed a well-defined mass of approximately 23 × 13 mm along the medial rectus (MR) muscle. It was isointense on T1W and hyperintense on T2W images with very minimal contrast enhancement (Figure 3). The patient initially consulted a local ophthalmic surgeon elsewhere, where it was initially diagnosed as cysticercosis and treated with albendazole and oral steroids.

panels.rationale: Single preoperative MSCT coronal image from case report of appendiceal cavernous hemangioma (classified as venous_malformation). In-text states focal calcifications of a thickened appendix, visible as punctate hyperdense focus, consistent with phlebolith/venous calculus vocabulary term.
panels.attribution_text: Rakić et al. Case report of incidental and asymptomatic appendiceal cavernous hemangioma.. International journal of surgery case reports 2025. doi:10.1016/j.ijscr.2025.111492. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative MSCT imaging.
in_text_mentions: Due to the rarity of this pathology, there are currently no established tools for straightforward diagnosis. panels.figure_caption: Enhanced magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the abdomen and pelvis with gadolinium. (a) Coronal view of an in-phase T1-weighted image identifying a large suprarenal mass measuring around 7.3 × 6.5 × 6 cm occupying the space of the right adrenal gland, showing a significant rim enhancement with marked vascularity. (b) Coronal view of a T2-weighted image identifying the similar right suprarenal mass with heterogeneous component inside it, possessing various signal intensities.
in_text_mentions: For better characterization of such adrenal lesion, a Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the abdomen with gadolinium was requested. Again showing was a mass in the right suprarenal space, measuring 7.3 × 6.5 × 6 cm, showing heterogeneous signal intensity on all sequences, predominately mildly increased on T2-weighted and predominately decreased signal on T1-weighted images, and no appreciable signal drop on the out-of-phase images. The lesion appeared inseparable from the lateral limb of the right adrenal gland and remained separate from the upper edge cortex of the right kidney (Figure 1).

Due to the size of the tumor, a shared decision was made to surgically remove the adrenal gland due to a potential risk of being an adrenocortical carcinoma. The patient therefore underwent a right radical adrenalectomy through an open subcostal incision. Intraoperatively, the adrenal was noticeably friable and tended to bleed on minimal manipulation, which was expected from the preoperative imaging done (Figure 1). No significant blood loss was encountered since complete dissection of the adrenal gland was done for better hemostatic control.

in_text_mentions: d tomography revealed a circular, inhomogeneous, honeycomb‐like tumor growing into the left nasal cavity. Magnetic resonance imaging detected a 21 × 14‐mm lobulated, heterogeneous enhancing mass in the left nasal bone and ethmoid bone (Figure 2). The mass spread into the surrounding subcutaneous tissue and damaged the bony wall of the nasolacrimal duct. Nasal endoscopy indicated swelling of the nasal mucosa covering the lacrimal sac (Figure 1). To rule out malignancy, an endoscopic biopsy was conducted in an outpatient setting, and the pathologist confirmed a diagnosis of cavernous hemangioma.

in_text_mentions: Follow-up and outcome: histopathological examination of the tissue shows vascular proliferation with large, congested vessels and gaping lumens, characteristic of a cavernous hemangioma. Immunohistochemical staining for EMA and S100 was negative, ruling out a neurofibroma and confirming the diagnosis of cavernous hemangioma (Figure 3A, B). The postoperative course was uncomplicated, with rapid and complete recovery of the motor deficit and the patient's ability to walk independently.

in_text_mentions: hard with bony particles, and covered with intact normal mucosa. There was a significant hemorrhage but it was controlled with nasal packaging. Blood transfusion was not needed. After excision of the lesion, nasal cavity was packed with merocel pad. The packing was removed on the second postoperative day. The postoperative course was uneventful. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of bony trabeculae and anastomosing vascular channels of cavernous pattern. Histological diagnosis was reported as osseous cavernous hemangioma (Figure 3). There was no evidence of recurrence at 1-year followup.

in_text_mentions: le endoscopy was performed and revealed active small bowel bleeding, originating most likely from the proximal- or mid-small bowel. Due to the recurrent GI bleeding that required multiple blood transfusions, the surgery team decided to perform a diagnostic laparoscopy that revealed the presence of a mass in the small intestine. Small bowel resection was performed (Figure 2), and the specimen was sent for histopathological analysis. A cavernous hemangioma, measuring 1.2 cm x 1 cm x 0.8 cm, with features of arteriovenous malformation, ulcer, and hemorrhage, was noted to be present (Figures 3-5).

in_text_mentions: endothelial cells, without atypia or mitosis. The stroma showed extensive fibrinous material in which many Liesegangs rings were observed. The rings were assembled in a lamellar fashion similar to psammoma bodies or a parasite egg (commonly, kidney worm). With an amorphous material in the middle, the central core was surrounded by a two-layered wall that stained negative with PAS and von Kossa (for calcium). The annular structure was nonbirefringent when viewed under polarized-light microscopy, and on immunohistochemistry, the cystic lining tested positive for CD34 and CD31 (Figures 3 and 4).

panels.figure_caption: a) Fibrous benign stroma (*) with dilated cavernous vessels and mature adipocyte cells in the periphery (**), H&E x4. b) The vessels filled with red blood cells (*). The endothelium and the stroma showed no signs of malignancy, H&E x10.
in_text_mentions: The pathological anatomy findings confirmed the diagnosis. Grossly, it was a 1,2x1x0.3 cm reddish mass with an elliptical shape. On section, a hemorrhagic-like surface was observed. The microscopic report described dilated vessels with a cavernous appearance, and the lumen was occupied by red blood cells. The stroma was fibrous with a benign appearance, and adipose cells were observed in the periphery (Figure 2 (Fig. 2)).

panels.figure_caption: Blue nodules with hemorrhagic crust and surrounding erythematous plaque noted on the lateral right knee consistent with venous malformation and angiokeratomas
in_text_mentions: Skin examination revealed (1) several blue nodules with hemorrhagic crust on the right lower extremity consistent with venous malformation and angiokeratoma (Figure 2); (2) one firm violaceous plaque with tenderness to palpation in the mid-tibial region consistent with phleboliths (Figure 3); and (3) several small (i.e., > 2 cm2) well-demarcated erythematous patches in the right popliteal fossa consistent with capillary malformation (Figure 4). Complete blood count (CBC) and basic metabolic panel (BMP)values were within normal limits. The patient was not taking any oral medications.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is HE x4 patient histology of adrenal cavernous hemangioma showing dilated vessels, matching dilated venous channels histology for venous_malformation. B: Panel B is HE x4 patient histology showing dilated tightly packed vessels demarcated from adrenal parenchyma, supporting venous malformation histology. C: Panel C is HE x40 patient histology showing endothelium-lined dilated vessels of adrenal cavernous hemangioma, matching dilated venous channels. D: Panel D is HE x40 patient histology grouped with C in caption describing endothelium-lined vessels of adrenal cavernous hemangioma.
panels.attribution_text: Kamel et al. Adrenal cavernous hemangioma: A rare cause of chronic lumbar pain - a case report.. International journal of surgery case reports 2024. doi:10.1016/j.ijscr.2024.109936. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Microscopic study images of an adrenal cavernous hemangioma. (A, B: HE staining ×4): Dilated and tightly packed vessels filled with clots and sometimes thrombi can be seen (A, Black Arrow). These vessels are well demarcated from the adjacent adrenal parenchyma (B, Black Asterisk) and divided by thin fibrous septa. (C, D: HE staining ×40): Vessels are lined by a single layer of regular endothelial cells (C, Black Arrow).
in_text_mentions: adrenal gland, surrounded by fat tissue, measuring 5.5 * 3.5 * 3 cm, with a 4-cm hemorrhagic lesion (Fig. 2). Histological study of the adrenal specimen concluded to an adrenal cavernous hemangioma (Fig. 3), which is a benign adrenal tumor. A rigorous and regular clinical follow-up of the patient was decided. Chronic lumbar pain - which was the chief complaint-, has completely vanished at sixth month follow-up. That reinforced the assumption of a causality link between the mass and the lumbar pain.Fig. 2Left adrenal gland with a hemorrhagic solid lesion corresponding to adrenal hemangioma.Fig

in_text_mentions: A pelvic MRI was ordered and demonstrated a pseudonodular lesion, 1.5 cm in size, arising from the anterior wall of the anal canal at 2 cm from the anal verge. The lesion appeared hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, suggestive of a vascular nature (Figure 1). There were no additional abnormal findings.

panels.rationale: Single IHC panel from patient with final diagnosis of combined lymphatic-venous malformation. CD31-positive lining of dilated thin-walled channels visibly shows venous component, matching dilated venous channels histology finding. [raw subtype: combined lymphatic-venous malformation]
panels.attribution_text: Perillo et al. A Rare Case of a Large Intra-Abdominal Lymphatic-Venous Malformation in a Young Woman Presenting to the Emergency Room with Abdominal Pain.. Reports (MDPI) 2025. doi:10.3390/reports8030183. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 7.
panels.figure_caption: The inner lining cells react to CD31 immunohistochemistry staining.
in_text_mentions: Immunohistochemical analysis revealed strong positivity for CD31, CD34, and podoplanin (D2-40), highlighting the coexistence of venous and lymphatic endothelial components [5]. This supported the final histological diagnosis of a combined lymphatic-venous malformation, in accordance with the 2018 ISSVA classification [4]. (Figure 6 and Figure 7).

in_text_mentions: le endoscopy was performed and revealed active small bowel bleeding, originating most likely from the proximal- or mid-small bowel. Due to the recurrent GI bleeding that required multiple blood transfusions, the surgery team decided to perform a diagnostic laparoscopy that revealed the presence of a mass in the small intestine. Small bowel resection was performed (Figure 2), and the specimen was sent for histopathological analysis. A cavernous hemangioma, measuring 1.2 cm x 1 cm x 0.8 cm, with features of arteriovenous malformation, ulcer, and hemorrhage, was noted to be present (Figures 3-5).

panels.figure_caption: Histological images, showing ectatic vascular spaces filled with blood, lined by flat endothelial cells without atypia and also areas with variable fibrosis, all compatible with a cavernous hemangioma of thyroid origin.
in_text_mentions: Pathological anatomy describes a well-circumscribed nodular lesion, consisting of ectatic vascular spaces filled with blood and lined by flat endothelial cells without atypia (Fig. 2). In addition, areas with variable fibrosis are identified, without histological signs of malignancy, all compatible with a cavernous hemangioma of thyroid origin. As an incidental finding, a well-differentiated 1.5-mm papillary microcarcinoma with free margins and no vascular or perineural invasion is found. With these results, the case is discussed again in a multidisciplinary committee, which decided follow-up.

in_text_mentions: nd difficulty in distinguishing between hemangioma and lymphatic malformation, we opted for contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck. The MRI revealed a well-defined lesion measuring 1.3 x 1.2 x 1.7 cm over the right base of the tongue that appeared homogeneously isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. The lesion did not involve the extrinsic muscles of the tongue but was adjacent to the vallecula region. Post-contrast images (T2) showed incomplete enhancement of the lesion at the right base of the tongue, with no apparent arterial supply toward the lesion (Figure 2).

Nerve fascicles and bony trabeculae were also present. These histological features were diagnostic of an intramuscular cavernous hemangioma (Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 6).

panels.figure_caption: Constructive Interference in Steady State (CISS) MRI demonstrating the relationship of the lesion to the cranial nerves. a: The proximal cisternal segments of the right facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerve complex are preserved (yellow arrow), with anterior displacement of cisternal segments by the lesion (red arrow). b: The proximal glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and accessory (XI) nerves are identified; however, their distal segments at the level of the right jugular foramen are obscured by the lesion (red arrow) on the right side.
in_text_mentions: Evaluation of the cranial nerves in CISS (Constructive Interference in Steady State) sequence demonstrated preservation of the proximal cisternal segments of the facial and vestibulocochlear nerve complex, with anterior displacement of their distal portions (Figures 3a, 3b).

in_text_mentions: An orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 16-mm diameter, well-circumscribed mass originating from left maxilla in close proximity to the zygomatic bone (Fig 1). The mass was on the left inferolateral orbital wall protruding toward orbital cavity and maxillary sinus (Fig 2). Intraorbital structures were reported to be intact without any sign of infiltration, compression, or displacement. The diagnosis was intraosseous cavernous hemangioma. Eosinophilic granuloma and fibrous dysplasia was considered in the differential diagnosis.

A: T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI orbit showing ill-defined intraconal/extraconal mass in article titled Retrobulbar Cavernous Hemangioma, curated as venous_malformation with captioned mass manifestation. B: T2-weighted MRI orbit showing ill-defined intraconal/extraconal mass corresponding to orbital venous malformation (retrobulbar cavernous hemangioma). C: DWI/ADC MRI orbit showing same ill-defined intraconal/extraconal mass of retrobulbar cavernous hemangioma curated as venous_malformation. D: Flair MRI orbit showing same ill-defined intraconal/extraconal mass of retrobulbar cavernous hemangioma curated as venous_malformation.

(C) Diffusion-weighted imaging/apparent diffusion coefficient image. (D) Flair image. (A-D) Showing an ill-defined mass involving both intraconal and extraconal spaces without any evidence of intracranial extension (yellow arrows).
in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) orbit and paranasal sinus confirmed the presence of an ill-defined mass involving both intraconal and extraconal spaces. There was a ballooning of the lamina papyracea giving appearance of apparent involvement of ethmoid sinus, but the frontal sinus appeared grossly normal. MRI brain was within normal limits without any evidence of intracranial extension of the mass (Figure 3A-3D, yellow arrows).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Coronal T1 gadolinium MRI of real patient showing well-defined enhancing lesion in inferior orbital rim. Disease attribution via disease-focused article title 'Unusual extraconal orbital location of a cavernous hemangioma' mapped to venous_malformation plus captioned lesion. No T1 MRI term in vocabulary so captured as proposed finding. Atypical due to unusual extraconal location stated in title. b: Coronal T2 MRI of real patient showing hyperintense well-defined inferior orbital rim lesion with capsule and low-intensity septation. Matches vocabulary T2 hyperintense lesion. Disease attribution via disease-focused title plus captioned manifestation. Atypical due to unusual extraconal location.
panels.attribution_text: Pacheco Callirgos et al. Unusual extraconal orbital location of a cavernous hemangioma.. GMS ophthalmology cases 2022. doi:10.3205/oc000204. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging of the coronal section. a) MRI – T1 gadolinium-enhanced showed a well-defined lesion in the inferior orbital rim that was enhanced with contrast. b) MRI – T2 showed a hyperintense lesion. The capsule is shown as well as low-intensity septation.
in_text_mentions: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed. It showed a well-localized mass with circumscribed edges and progressive enhancement with gadolinium in sequence T1 (Figure 1a (Fig. 1)) and homogeneous enhancement in sequence T2 (Figure 1b (Fig. 1)).

panels.rationale: Sagittal MRI of infraorbital/maxillary mass diagnosed in-text as intraosseous cavernous hemangioma in article titled Intraosseous cavernous hemangioma mapped to venous_malformation; yellow-arrow annotated lesion corresponds to well-circumscribed mass, visually consistent with lobulated MRI lesion vocabulary term; rare maxillary location supports atypical.
panels.attribution_text: Kaya et al. Intraosseous cavernous hemangioma: a rare presentation in maxilla.. Eplasty 2014. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Sagittal MRI image of the infraorbital lesion.
in_text_mentions: An orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 16-mm diameter, well-circumscribed mass originating from left maxilla in close proximity to the zygomatic bone (Fig 1). The mass was on the left inferolateral orbital wall protruding toward orbital cavity and maxillary sinus (Fig 2). Intraorbital structures were reported to be intact without any sign of infiltration, compression, or displacement. The diagnosis was intraosseous cavernous hemangioma. Eosinophilic granuloma and fibrous dysplasia was considered in the differential diagnosis.
